Getting Started with Flyway

Introduction

Keeping database changes in sync across environments can be a pain. Developers often rely on ad hoc SQL scripts or manual updates, which leads to errors, confusion, and broken builds. Flyway helps solve this by bringing version control to your database schema — just like Git does for your code.

In this post, I’ll show you how to get started with Flyway: how to structure your project, setting up migrations, and running them safely against your database. Whether you’re working solo or in a team, Flyway makes tracking and deploying database changes a lot easier.

Flyway supports a number of widely used databases such as Aurora MySQL, Aurora PostgreSQL, CockroachDB, Databricks, MariaDB, MongoDB, MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, Redshift, Snowflake, SQLite, SQL Server and TimescaleDB.

Migration File Naming

Flyway expects a specific naming convention:

  • Versioned migrations: V001__InitialSchema.sql
  • Undo migrations: U001__InitialSchema.sql (This is a commercial feature)
  • Repeatable migrations: R__RefreshViews.sql

I would recommend using triple-digit versioning (001, 002, etc.) to keep things orderly as your schema grows.

Example files in data/sql/:

V001__InitialSchema.sql
V002__Seed.sql
V003__Plays.sql
V004__MostPlays.sql

Keep the filenames meaningful. This will help others (and your future self) understand what each migration is doing at a glance.

Project Setup

Before diving in, make sure your environment is ready:

  • Docker: We’ll use containers to run Postgres and Flyway.
  • Go: Our backend API is written in Go.
  • ASDF (recommended): For managing multiple runtime versions easily (Go, Node, etc.).
  • DB GUI: Tools like TablePlus or Azure Data Studio make inspecting and querying the database easier.

I’ve attached a GitHub project for you to use https://github.com/DavidHaylock/getting-started-with-flyway

Fauxify

Welcome to Fauxify — our intentionally bad Spotify clone. We’re going to incrementally build out the database using Flyway migrations, and wire it into a Go API.

.
├── Makefile
├── apps
│   ├── api                  
│   │   └── routes           
│   └── fauxify              
├── data                     
│   └── sql                  
├── .env                     
├── docker-compose.pg.yaml  
├── docker-compose.flyway.yaml

Spinning Up the Database

Start by launching the Postgres container:

docker compose -f docker-compose.pg.yaml up

This sets up a clean Postgres instance using secrets from your .env file. At this point, the database will be empty — just the default public schema exists.

Flyway Migration Setup

We use Flyway to manage our schema migrations.

Inside the data/ folder you will find the following:

  • flyway.conf — base Flyway config. This sets up two schemas: one for tracking Flyway’s internal metadata, and one for our actual app data. The baselineOnMigrate=true option is useful for applying Flyway to existing databases that weren’t previously managed by it — it avoids errors if metadata tables don't yet exist.
flyway.schemas=flyway,fauxify
flyway.baselineOnMigrate=true
flyway.validateMigrationNaming=true
  • deploy.sh — runs the migration process. This script builds the JDBC URL and runs the flyway migrate command using the values from your .env file.
#!/bin/bash
set -e

DATABASE_URL="jdbc:postgresql://$POSTGRES_HOST:$POSTGRES_PORT/$POSTGRES_DB"
echo "DB URL: $DATABASE_URL"

flyway migrate -X \
  -url=$DATABASE_URL \
  -user=$POSTGRES_USER \
  -password=$POSTGRES_PASSWORD \
  -locations="filesystem:sql" \
  -baselineOnMigrate=true \
  -connectRetries=60
  • Dockerfile — This image copies in the config, script, and SQL folder and sets the entrypoint to execute the migration script.
FROM flyway/flyway:latest as db-init

WORKDIR /app

ARG FLYWAY_EDITION
ENV FLYWAY_EDITION="community"

COPY ./flyway.conf ./flyway.conf
COPY ./deploy.sh ./deploy.sh
COPY ./sql ./sql

ENTRYPOINT [ "./deploy.sh" ]
  • sql/ — all your migration scripts live here

Make the project

It’s worth saying now after each sql file run make migrate .

Create the V001__IntialSchema.sql file. We’ll define our basic tables here. We have artists, albums, eps and songs.

BEGIN;
    CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS fauxify;

    CREATE TABLE fauxify.artists (
        id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
        name VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
        country VARCHAR(255) NULL,
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
        updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    );
    
    CREATE INDEX IDX_NAME ON fauxify.artists (name);

    CREATE TABLE fauxify.albums (
        id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
        title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
        artist_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES fauxify.artists(id),
        release_date DATE,
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
        updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    );

    CREATE TABLE fauxify.eps (
        id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
        title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
        artist_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES fauxify.artists(id),
        release_date DATE,
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
        updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    );

    CREATE TABLE fauxify.songs (
        id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
        title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
        album_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES fauxify.albums(id),
        track_number INT NOT NULL,
        duration_seconds INT,
        plays INT DEFAULT 0,
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
        updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    );

    -- only one instance of a track number per album.
    ALTER TABLE fauxify.songs ADD CONSTRAINT unique_album_track UNIQUE (album_id, track_number);

    CREATE INDEX IDX_TITLE ON fauxify.songs (title);
    CREATE INDEX IDX_ALBUM ON fauxify.songs (album_id);
COMMIT;

Run make migrate

If you open your DB GUI and open the flyway schema you’ll see that flyway has recorded our migration.

Open the fauxify schema and voila our tables appear.

This will seed the db with some values.

We want to be able to track users plays of the songs to build a dynamic most played list. So that in the future we could tailor song suggestions.

Let’s go make a new table, Create a V003__Plays.sql file and add the following. We’ll create a new table whilst dropping the original column from the songs table.

BEGIN;
    CREATE TABLE fauxify.song_analytics (
        id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
        song_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES fauxify.songs(id),
        play_time INT NOT NULL,
        user_id UUID NULL,
        created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
    );

    ALTER TABLE fauxify.songs DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS plays;
COMMIT;

In our scenario we’ll need to seed some data for the plays. Create a R__Plays.sql file. This will be run each time the migrations happen.

CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS "uuid-ossp";

DO $$ 
DECLARE
  song_id UUID;
  song_duration_seconds INT;
  random_position_seconds INT;
  random_created_at TIMESTAMP;
  random_song RECORD;
BEGIN
  FOR i IN 1..100000 LOOP
    SELECT id, title, duration_seconds INTO random_song
    FROM fauxify.songs
    ORDER BY RANDOM()
    LIMIT 1;

    song_id := random_song.id;
    song_duration_seconds := random_song.duration_seconds;
    random_position_seconds := FLOOR(RANDOM() * song_duration_seconds);
    random_created_at := CURRENT_TIMESTAMP - INTERVAL '1 day' * FLOOR(RANDOM() * 1200);

    INSERT INTO fauxify.song_analytics (id, song_id, play_time, user_id, created_at)
    VALUES (gen_random_uuid(), song_id, random_position_seconds, gen_random_uuid(), random_created_at);
  END LOOP;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

Again if you look at the flyway schema it will have logged our migrations.

Now we’ve got our data, we need a dynamic table. Create a V004__MostPlays.sql file. Add the following.

BEGIN;

CREATE VIEW fauxify.most_plays AS
SELECT
    s.title AS song_title,
    a.title AS album_title,
    ar.name AS artist_name,
    COUNT(p.id) AS play_count
FROM
    fauxify.songs s
JOIN
    fauxify.albums a ON s.album_id = a.id
JOIN
    fauxify.artists ar ON a.artist_id = ar.id
LEFT JOIN
    fauxify.song_analytics p ON s.id = p.song_id
GROUP BY
    s.id, a.id, ar.id
ORDER BY
    play_count DESC;

COMMIT;

To simplify things we could amalgamate the albums and eps tables, but we need to transfer the data across.

Create a V005__RemoveEps.sql file and add the following.

BEGIN;

ALTER TABLE fauxify.albums
 ADD COLUMN is_ep BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;

INSERT INTO
 fauxify.albums (id, title, artist_id, release_date, is_ep, created_at, updated_at)
SELECT
 id,
 title,
 artist_id,
 release_date,
 TRUE,
 created_at,
 updated_at
FROM
 fauxify.eps;

DROP TABLE fauxify.eps;

ALTER TABLE fauxify.songs
ADD CONSTRAINT fk_album
FOREIGN KEY (album_id)
REFERENCES fauxify.albums(id);

COMMIT;

But, to prove the undo capabilities, let’s revert the change. If you use the commercial licence you can use the U prefix as long as the version number matches. For the community licence you need to perform an V migration.

BEGIN;

  CREATE TABLE fauxify.eps (
    id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    title VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
    artist_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES fauxify.artists(id),
    release_date DATE,
    created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
  );

INSERT INTO
 fauxify.eps (id, title, artist_id, release_date, created_at, updated_at)
SELECT
 id,
 title,
 artist_id,
 release_date,
 created_at,
 updated_at
FROM
 fauxify.albums
WHERE 
  is_ep = TRUE;

ALTER TABLE fauxify.albums
 DROP COLUMN is_ep;

COMMIT;

What about if we try run the same migration twice?

The benefit of Flyway is that it checks the flyway table for previous migrations and skips over the files, if no new migrations are found flyway will just return.

Conclusion

Flyway brings structure and sanity to database migrations. It helps teams avoid the pain of manual SQL sync and makes rollouts safer and faster. Add it to your toolkit!
